messages.subject: Advice sought for ordered probit model
messages.subject_clean: Advice sought for ordered probit model
messages.body_plain:
I would like to canvas the Zelig list for suggestions, comments and guidance in applying

Zelig's ordered probit model to some chess performance data.



Preamble:

The late former world chess champion Bobby Fischer alleged that players from the former Soviet 

Union had colluded when playing against him.

This claim is investigated using probit analysis in the following paper by Moul and Nye:



[

Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization

Volume 70, Issues 1-2, May 2009, Pages 10-21  



Did the Soviets collude? A statistical analysis of championship chess 1940–1978 



Charles C. Moul(a),  and John V.C. Nye (b) 



(a) Miami University, Oxford, Ohio 45056, United States

(b) George Mason University, Fairfax, VA 22030, United States





Received 27 November 2007;  revised 30 January 2009;  accepted 30 January 2009.

Abstract

We expand the set of outcomes considered by the tournament literature to include draws and use 

games from post-war chess tournaments to see whether strategic behavior can be important in 

such scenarios. In particular, we examine whether players from the former Soviet Union acted 

as a cartel in international all-play-all tournaments – intentionally drawing against one 

another in order to focus effort on non-Soviet opponents – to maximize the chance of some 

Soviet winning. Using data from international qualifying tournaments as well as USSR national 

tournaments, we consider several tests for collusion. Our results are inconsistent with Soviet 

competition but consistent with Soviet draw-collusion that yielded substantial benefits to the 

cartel. Simulations of the period's five premier international competitions (the FIDE 

Candidates tournaments) suggest that the observed Soviet sweep was a 60%-probability event 

under collusion but only a 25%-probability event had the Soviet players not colluded.

]





The advent of powerful chess computer programs and miniature receiving devices has in recent 

years led to allegations of cheating via surreptitious computer assistance.



I am interested in applying Zelig's ordered probit model to predict the probability

of a player winning or achieving any particular finishing position in a chess

tournament. My interest is partly to learn Zelig's probit model, partly forensic, with the 

possibility of extending the method to look at other competitions.



Extensive data for chess competitions is available online and in chess game databases in the following formats, amongst others.



FIN = Finishing position

TITLE: GM = Grandmaster, other, lesser titles possible eg IM: International Master, FM: FIDE 

Master.

RATING: This is a player rating generated by FIDE the controlling body for international 

chess.

  These ratings are derived by an iterative process developed by Prof Arpad Elo from an 

arbitrary base rating.

  A higher rating implies a stronger player. Small rating differences circa 10 points are not 

considered significant.

  Using the outcomes of competitions player Ratings are recalculated at regular intervals by 

FIDE. They are important in the awarding of titles, in professional players getting invitations to the best and most lucrative tournaments and are a measure of player strength of keen interest to both amateur and professional players.



Here is a typical example of a recent event, only the top ten finishing players shown:



16th ORDIX Open Mainz (GER), 1-2 August 2009							

									

FIN	PLAYER			TITLE	COUNTRY	RATING	WINS	DRAWS	LOSSES	POINTS

1	Mamedyarov, Shakhriyar	GM	AZE	2717	9	2	0	10

2	Naiditsch, Arkadij	GM	GER	2697	9	1	1	9.5

3	Akopian, Vladimir	GM	ARM	2712	8	3	0	9.5

4	Gashimov, Vugar		GM	AZE	2740	9	1	1	9.5

5	Moiseenko, Alexander	GM	UKR	2682	8	2	1	9

6	Guliyev, Namig		GM	AZE	2555	9	0	2	9

7	Riazantsev, Alexander	GM	RUS	2647	8	2	1	9

8	Nakamura, Hikaru	GM	USA	2710	8	1	2	8.5

9	Sargissian, Gabriel	GM	ARM	2683	8	1	2	8.5

10	Bacrot, Etienne		GM	FRA	2721	7	3	1	8.5



For the ordered probit model the dependent variable is FIN.

Using as a sorce of test data many such result tables as above I want to develop a probit model that could be used to predict the outcome of an upcoming event or of a hold-out data set ie the 

probability of a particular competitor finishing 1st, 2nd....etc.



Theory tells us to expect that higher rated players ought to out-perform lower rated players

so one independent variable of interest is RATING.

A player's TITLE ought to be a useful independent variable as theory expects that a player with a higher title should finish ahead of a player with a lesser title.



Young, rapidly improving players could be expected to out-perform their rating so an 

independent variable of AGE could be useful (DOB of players is usually known).



Other possible independent variables may be related to RECENT RESULTS that is: how well has

the  player been performing recently or WORLD RANK, the rank the player occupies on FIDE's list of Ratings.



There have been alternative rating algorithms proposed due to some perceived weaknesses with 

the Elo method. With this in mind I would envisage another use of a probit model would be to 

test alternatve rating methods to see which best predicts the outcome of competitions.



Several questions come to mind:

1. Should I normalize variables such as RATING?

2. If so, should I normalize within each event or over all events in my test database?

3. Is it advisable to create a variable TITLE_GM which takes value 1 if player has GM title, 0 

otherwise and likewise for TITLE_IM, TITLE_FM?



Any assistance or comments as to setting up the probit model or preprocessing the data etc 

greatly appreciated!

Cheers Peter Jameson

messages.subject: Error using Zelig, Amelia & normal.survey-model
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to combine multiple imputation and sample weights using
Amelia & Zelig's normal.survey model. Example code-snippet:

[[
x <- (dataframe, including weight-variable "weight")
a.out <- amelia(x, m=5, idvars=c("weight"))
a.mi <- mi(imp$imputations)
fit <- zelig(support ~ sex, model="normal.survey", data=a.mi, weights=~weight)
]]

Unfortunately, I get the error: "Error in svyglm.survey.design(formula
= support ~ sex, design = list(cluster = list( :   all variables must
be in design= argument". It does return a fitted model after it prints
the error.

I can use svyglm() directly and imputationList() & MIcombine() from
the mitools package to analyze Amelia's imputed datasets, for the same
formula:

[[
a.mi <- imputationList(a.out$imputations)
d <- svydesign(id=~1, data=a.mi)  #passing an ids=~1 parameter to
zelig() does not help
results <- with(d, svyglm(support ~ sex))
MIcombine(results)
]]

But the output is less complete than that of Zelig.

Am I doing something wrong, or is it not possible to use imputed
datasets from Amelia together with sample weights?

salutations,

Maarten

messages.subject: simulations with a mediator
messages.body_plain:
Dear Zelig Folk,

I have a problem that you may have dealt with: mediating effects. Here's a
very simple version of the problem:

We have mock jury data in which:

Verdict (V) ~ Factual Perception (FP) + Egalitarianism (E)


Simple, right?  Except that E influences V both directly and indirectly
through an influence on FP. So we really have two equations:


V ~ FP + E  and  FP ~ E


Since both V & FP are dependent on E, I should be able to simulate a
distribution of FP with E set to X *and* a distribution of V with E set to X
and FP set to sim(FP[E=X]).

The way I'm trying to do this by simulating 1000 values for FP with E set to
X.  Now I have FPsim[1...1000].  Now I want to simulate V by setting E to X
and FP set to FPsim[1...1000].

So my questions are: Is that reasonable way to estimate direct & indirect
effects in theory?  How would you go about doing it in practice?

Don

messages.subject: Re: your mail
messages.body_plain:
Hi Brad,

   Thanks for your email.  In zelig, we do not support "subset" command, 
but instead we have "by" command where the model will be fitted separately 
to each subclass defined by it.

I hope this helps,
Kosuke

-- 
Department of Politics
Princeton University
http://imai.princeton.edu

messages.subject: num < 8
messages.body_plain:
Dear Zelig Folk,
For a few applications, I'd like to run a single simulation.  I thought I
might do this by setting num=1, but if I set num to anything less than 8, I
get the following error:

> Error in qi.polr(object[[1]], simpar = simpar, x = as.matrix(x), x1 = if
> (!is.null(x1)) as.matrix(x1)) :

  subscript out of bounds


Except when I set num to either 1 or 2, in which case I get the following
error:

Error in matrix(rnorm(p * n), n) : invalid 'ncol' value (too large or NA)


It's not all that important to what I'm doing, but I'm curious if anyone
knows why this happens or if there's anything that can be done about it.

Cheers, Don
